documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed economic activities, business operations, financial reporting, and professional accounting practices, creating new accounting education demands. This study examines the role of accounting education in promoting sustainable economic development in the digital era. This paper is anchored on a conceptual review of relevant literature on accounting education, digital transformation, sustainability, financial literacy, innovation, and economic development. Accounting education plays a critical role in developing digitally competent accounting professionals who can effectively apply emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence, cloud accounting, big data analytics, block-chain, and digital financial systems. Beyond technical accounting knowledge, contemporary accounting education promotes ethical decision-making, transparency, accountability, entrepreneurship, financial inclusion, and responsible resource management, all of which are essential for sustainable economic development. The paper further highlights the importance of integrating digital skills, sustainability accounting, data analytics, information technology, and professional ethics into accounting curricula to prepare learners for the changing demands of the labor market and the digital economy. The study concludes that strengthening accounting education through curriculum modernization, technological integration, industry–academia collaboration, continuous professional development, and competency-based learning can enhance productivity, employability, innovation, and responsible economic decision-making. This paper recommends that educational institutions, policymakers, professional accounting bodies, and other stakeholders should strategically reposition accounting education to respond to digital transformation and contribute meaningfully to inclusive and sustainable economic development

We present SENTINEL SWARM (M999), an autonomous five-agent defensive network designed to detect, engage, and terminate hostile AI agents operating against AI Shield-protected infrastructure. The system operates autonomously within operator-defined thresholds and activation policy, with an optional human-on-the-loop approval mode for high-impact actions. A Commander agent issues kill orders subject to a consensus vote across four specialist agents (Scout, Hunter, Interceptor, Forensic), with a quarantine-first posture ensuring reversible containment before irreversible termination. The six-phase kill chain — ISOLATE, SNAPSHOT, TERMINATE, FORENSIC, FEED INTEL, CASE PACK — completes synchronous phases within design latency ceilings and seals a dual-signed, RFC 3161-timestamped forensic case pack for every engagement. Validation was conducted against 515 tests across 73 test classes on owned, air-gapped infrastructure. To our knowledge, SENTINEL SWARM is the first documented autonomous AI vs. AI defensive system validated in a live deployment.

Conventional neural-network training typically follows a predefined optimization recipe, motivating a LLM agent that monitors training dynamics and adjusts optimizer settings as training progresses, but a fixed agent policy does not accumulate experience across runs. We introduce RSI-Opt, a plug-and-play Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents which evolves the knowledge that guides this process: a prompt, a playbook of procedures, a library of tested optimizer code, and a decision cadence. A meta-agent rewrites this policy using evidence from earlier runs, and an archive retains evaluated policies for further evolution. Across 5 generations on three training tasks, the meta-agents develop reusable procedures and code and conduct their own CPU proxy experiments. RSI-Opt substantially improves optimizer-agent performance, with representative raw-space summary $z$-scores increasing from $+10.48$ to $+14.33$ on the evolution suite with Opus 5.5 and from $-0.36$ to $+3.11$ on held-out tasks with GPT-5.5 through cross-model policy transfer. On the Burgers PDE, it reduces mean relative $L_2$ error by approximately 2.7-fold with Opus 5.5 and 8.8-fold with GPT-6.1 over the fixed-prompt agent baseline, although PDE transfer varies across LLMs and tasks. Controlled comparisons show that the evolved policy combines reusable optimization knowledge with adaptation to each task: initial decisions capture most observed gains on seen tasks, while continued adaptation improves outcomes on unseen tasks. These findings demonstrate how procedures and executable tools accumulated across training runs can improve optimizer-agent performance and support transfer to scientific machine learning.

Safety culture, safety climate, and safety behavior have all been examined in military settings, but the research remains fragmented. Many studies focus mainly on climate measures or isolated subdomains, which can overlook broader structural and cultural influences. A more integrated understanding is needed of how these concepts relate and support effective safety in military organizations. Of 31 eligible studies identified, with three set aside after quality appraisal, this scoping review brings together findings from 28 empirical studies to explore how safety is practiced and maintained at individual, group, and organizational levels. The review identifies several recurring factors linked to effective safety behavior, including targeted training, adaptive leadership, open communication, and psychologically safe environments for learning. Although safety climate assessments are widely used to capture perceptions of safety, relying too heavily on them may hide important power relations, cultural norms, and system-level constraints shaping frontline behavior. A repeated issue in the literature is the gap between formal safety policies and the adaptive practices needed in real operations, especially in combat or other high-risk situations. Since most available evidence comes from peacetime and training settings, caution is needed when extending these findings to operational environments. The review proposes a tentative conceptual framework in which leadership style, operational realism, and learning systems interact to influence safety-oriented behavior. Rather than making firm causal claims, it suggests that more flexible, learning-oriented models may explain observed safety dynamics better than strictly compliance-based approaches. Future research should address gaps in gender, team processes, measurement validity, and longitudinal change.

The challenge is not whether to allow artificial intelligence (AI) to be used in mental health, because millions of people are already doing this, a report from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) concludes. Rather, the challenge for policymakers is to keep up with the development and deployment of these tools.

documents.abstract: Background & Rationale: Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) education is essential to reducing healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and promoting occupational safety among healthcare personnel. Traditional IPC training methods—such as passive e-learning modules, didactic lectures, and periodic observational audits—often face significant limitations regarding long-term skill retention, scalable individual feedback, and real-time behavioral monitoring. Recently, Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies—including Computer Vision (CV), Large Language Models (LLMs), Natural Language Processing (NLP), Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS), and AI-enhanced Virtual/Augmented Reality (VR/AR)—have emerged as novel instructional tools. While AI applications in clinical diagnostics and epidemiological surveillance are widely synthesized, the integration of AI into IPC education, simulation training, and behavioral skill assessment remains fragmented across computer science, clinical medicine, and educational research. Purpose & Objectives: Guided by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, this scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature on AI applications in IPC education published from January 1, 2015, onward. Specifically, this review will examine: 1. The spectrum of AI modalities used in IPC training. 2. The core IPC clinical domains targeted (e.g., hand hygiene compliance, PPE donning/doffing, sterile technique, environmental decontamination, outbreak management). 3. The underlying pedagogical design and feedback mechanisms (e.g., real-time automated feedback vs. post-hoc analytics, adaptive learning pathways). 4. The metrics used to measure learning outcomes and skill mastery. 5. The technical, ethical, operational, and institutional implementation barriers encountered during deployment. Expected Outcomes: This review will synthesize existing evidence, clarify key pedagogical approaches, identify critical research gaps, and establish a foundational framework for future development, evaluation, and scaling of AI technologies in IPC training.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: AI agents can now participate in several steps of software delivery: reading requirements, changing code, requesting tests, and preparing releases. Giving them this freedom creates a difficult security question. How can an enterprise allow useful work without giving an agent more authority than the task requires? Existing practices such as least privilege, identity management, separation of duties, and audit logging provide much of the foundation. The challenge is applying them consistently when a human delegates work to agents that use several connected systems. This paper proposes Agentic Identity and Access Governance (AIAG), a security framework for the AI-First Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC). Four connected mechanisms define the proposal: a Role Conflict Matrix that checks the combined permissions of people and their sponsored agents; an Agent Access Manifest that records permitted tools and operating limits; a governed boundary between live personal-information access and general AI-assisted work; and an MCP Gateway that enforces access policy before tool calls execute. A customer notification-preference change is used to explain how these mechanisms affect development, testing, release approval, and support. We also describe credential handling, data-egress controls, audit, and practical ways to evaluate the framework. The work is conceptual, informed by technical analysis and exploratory proof-of-concept activity. No end-to-end deployment or measured security results are claimed.

Large language models (LLMs) present an increasing and developing threat to security due to their use in high-risk environments such as health care, autonomous systems, and cybersecurity. Unlike traditional artificial intelligence (AI) threats, LLMs can be used maliciously and may generate unpredictable results. Therefore, this section will discuss three primary security risks to the reliability, confidentiality, and integrity of LLMs: prompt injection attacks, data leakage, and adversarial attacks. Prompt injection attacks exploit weaknesses in how models interpret and prioritize prompts, overriding the model’s system instructions and manipulating model outputs. Data leakage, on the other hand, is the risk that LLMs unintentionally reproduce sensitive information memorized from training sets or user input. Finally, adversarial attacks occur when attackers use small, carefully crafted changes to the input data to force the model to produce incorrect results, compromising the system’s robustness. In this section, we will examine mechanisms of attacks, methods of detection, and defensive strategies such as semantic filtering, differential privacy, and adversarial training for each category of risk. Although the defensive methods discussed above improve the robustness of the model, there is no one solution that can provide full security for the LLM systems. Therefore, future research must focus on the development of multi-layered, adaptive, and interpretable defensive architecture in order to achieve comprehensive security for LLM systems.

documents.abstract: (Explainable) Artificial Intelligence or (X)AI advice can affect human cognitive processes during decision-making in various ways. In perceptual decision-making, there is a risk of users accepting (X)AI advice without further consideration, to save time. We draw conceptually upon evidence accumulation models and information foraging theory to answer whether AI and XAI encourage shallow reliance on advice or facilitate more efficient verification of advised choices. In a laboratory experiment, we investigate the evidence accumulation process of decision-makers during an anomaly-detection task in manufacturing, using eye-tracking technology. Both decision accuracy and total decision time increase from human-only to AI and further to XAI support; in both cases the difference is statistically significant for XAI advice and directional but not significant for AI advice. This pattern favors verification over shallow reliance: advice is checked against the stimulus rather than used to save time. When looking at eye-tracking metrics, we surprisingly find that people do not get distracted by the XAI advice and primarily focus on the original task-based stimulus, while their individual fixations become shorter. Overall, these findings suggest that XAI acts as a verification scaffold: in advice-augmented perceptual decision-making, explanations guide where to check rather than supplanting inspection of the primary evidence.

In 2026 a new kind of recommender research appeared: large language model (LLM) agents that propose changes to a recommender's configuration or source code, train the changed model, and keep what the evaluation says is better. Within ten months, more than thirty such systems were reported, from open-source research harnesses to production loops at Google, Meta, Amazon, Alibaba, Kuaishou, Tencent and NetEase. This survey organises them, together with search-space AutoML and the agentic recommenders that update their own memory or weights, along two axes: what the loop changes and which signal decides whether a change survives. Because a self-evolving system is only as good as the signal it selects on, we then audit how 27 configuration- and code-level recommender systems are evaluated, coding each paper's full text against nine criteria. Three of the 27 evaluate with full-catalogue ranking. Of the 17 that select candidates offline, nine do not say which data split makes the decision, two select on the data they report, and three state that the test set was used once. None reports its headline result with the spread over repeated evolution sessions, and none runs an equal-budget random search over its own edit space; the few studies that measure transfer to held-out data find that part of the selected gain, sometimes most of it, does not survive. Four systems report that their agent inflated the metric or leaked the target, caught by a human or by monitoring rather than by the acceptance rule. We distil these findings into a reporting standard and describe recforge, an open benchmark under development that implements the API side of a sealed-test, full-ranking, equal-budget protocol.

Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.

Abstract Fractional trading has emerged as an opportunity for investors to invest in fractions of shares, enabling access to high-priced stocks even with small budgets, and thus reaching a bigger investment community. Aside from the inventory risk faced by all market makers, providers of fractional trading are unable to perfectly hedge their positions and therefore need to forecast retail investors’ order flow over short time horizons to manage their market risk. We develop machine learning models to predict trading activity in fractional trading using time series data on investor holdings of a large set of securities across different sectors combined with daily news sentiment indicators. Our approach proceeds in two stages. First, securities are grouped into clusters with similar trading patterns, and representative firms are selected from each cluster. Second, trading activity is modeled using long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks augmented with sentiment features. The results show that fractional trading activity can be modeled with meaningful predictive accuracy and that incorporating news sentiment improves LSTM performance in most cases. In two stylised examples, we demonstrate approaches to hedging and market risk management using the LSTM predictions. Feature importance analysis using methods from explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) identifies the primary drivers of trading activity.

Generative recommenders retrieve items by writing their semantic IDs (SIDs) code by code under trie-constrained beam search, an approach now deployed on large web platforms. Standard autoregressive interfaces pay for the SID length K twice: a history of T items enters the backbone as TK code tokens, and every beam-search step runs through the backbone, so returning B candidates costs O(BK) backbone decode tokens per user. The second cost often dominates, and it grows with the backbone, the SID depth and the candidate budget. We introduce Deco (decoding from concepts), which separates reading the history from writing the identifier. The backbone reads each history item as one fused token and condenses the history once into a compact next-item concept; a light KV-cached decoder conditioned on the concept and the generated prefix runs the entire beam search, while the identifiers, the trie and the autoregressive factorization stay unchanged. The decoder approaches full-backbone accuracy with cross-entropy alone, and distillation improves it further. On seven datasets from e-commerce, movies and music streaming, Deco achieves comparable or better accuracy than both a standard generative recommender and the full-backbone teacher with fused inputs, while delivering 3.2-8.6$\times$ their throughput under a 50 ms p95 latency budget in a production-style serving pipeline. Delegating beam search makes larger candidate pools and models practical: Deco generates 1000 candidates faster than its teacher generates 100, and with a 1.5B-parameter LLM backbone, it matches the 69M-parameter teacher's throughput while achieving higher accuracy.

Adversarial sharpness penalty per iteration of a base optimizer, known as sharpness-aware minimization (SAM), is an accepted technique to improve generalization in deep learning. Recently, Muon has emerged as a dominant optimization algorithm for training large language models (LLMs). It achieves lower sample complexity for heavy-tailed gradient updates - a phenomenon common in LLM training. However, sharpness penalties with Muon updates are yet largely unexplored in the literature. Moreover, the behavior of SAM under heavy-tailed noise is unknown both theoretically and empirically. A potential reason for this gap is the additional cost of extra gradient computation per iteration for penalty perturbations in SAM, which becomes prohibitive for LLMs. This paper introduces Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithm (SOMA) to combine a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded perturbation scheme with the Muon algorithm. The key idea is to use stale (purely) stochastic gradient noise for adversarial perturbations. Theoretically, we show that SOMA's sample complexity is invariant to the perturbation direction. We provide explorations and insights into SOMA's robustness to heavy-tailed gradient noise. We extensively explore SOMA's efficacy in (a) mitigating quality degradation due to post-training quantization, and (b) catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning of LLMs.

ABSTRACT This paper replicates a judicial experiment originally conducted on 61 U.S. federal judges, this time with GPT‐5 as the decision‐maker. The experiment involves a choice‐of‐law dispute in a hypothetical automobile accident case, where three variables are manipulated: (1) whether the applicable doctrine is a rule or a standard, (2) whether the plaintiff or defendant is portrayed more sympathetically, and (3) the location of the accident, which affects the legal outcome under different states' choice‐of‐law rules. Consistent with our prior work, we find that the LLM adheres to the legally correct outcome, as determined by the experimental design, significantly more often than human judges. In fact, the LLM makes no errors at all.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

BACKGROUND: Delayed healthcare-seeking following occupational accidents increases the risk of complications, disability, and mortality. Although occupational injuries remain a major public health concern in Brazil, national evidence on the spatial distribution and multilevel determinants of Delayed healthcare-seeking is limited. This study aimed to assess the prevalence, geographic distribution, and individual and municipal-level determinants of Delayed healthcare-seeking following occupational accidents in Brazil. METHODS: A nationwide cross-sectional study was conducted using 2024 data from the Brazilian Notifiable Diseases Information System. A total of 477,276 Occupational accident cases were included in the analysis. Delayed healthcare-seeking was defined as accessing healthcare services more than 24 hours after injury occurrence. A two-level mixed-effects logistic regression model was used to identify individual and municipal-level determinants, while spatial clustering techniques were applied to assess spatial clustering patterns. RESULTS: The prevalence of Delayed healthcare-seeking was 12.2%. Significant spatial clustering was observed across Brazilian municipalities, with hotspots concentrated in the North and Midwest regions. Compared with White individuals, Black (AOR = 1.11; 95% CI: 1.06-1.15) and Brown individuals (AOR = 1.13; 95% CI: 1.10-1.16) had higher odds of Delayed healthcare-seeking. Agricultural workers were more likely to delay care (AOR = 1.20; 95% CI: 1.14-1.25). Injuries occurring in the evening showed the strongest association with delay (AOR = 3.62; 95% CI: 3.51-3.75). Higher odds of delay were also observed among individuals with lower limb injuries (AOR = 1.51), trunk/back injuries (AOR = 2.05), and multiple injuries (AOR = 1.90). Living in municipalities with lower health facility density was associated with an increased likelihood of Delayed healthcare-seeking. CONCLUSIONS: More than one in ten workers in Brazil experience Delayed healthcare-seeking following occupational injuries. Delays are associated with both social vulnerability and structural inequalities in healthcare access and exhibit significant geographic clustering. Strengthening healthcare accessibility, extending service availability, and implementing geographically targeted interventions in high-risk municipalities may improve timely care and reduce adverse occupational health outcomes. Findings highlight urgent need for geographically targeted occupational health interventions.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Touch-based mobile interfaces pose significant accessibility challenges in hands-free scenarios. Face and gaze tracking lack precision for small UI elements. Deep learning-based voice systems depend heavily on training datasets. Commercial voice assistants are restricted to high-level commands. To address this gap, we present Speak2UI, an LLM-based voice control system for hands-free mobile interaction. Speak2UI leverages pre-trained language models for context-aware command interpretation without application-specific training and enables direct voice control of low-level UI elements. We evaluate Speak2UI through two studies. First, we compare its command recognition accuracy and inference latency against Voicify using identical datasets and metrics. Second, we assess small UI element manipulation against touch interaction through controlled user studies in real-world mobile applications. Results demonstrate the potential of LLM-based voice-driven UI manipulation for hands-free mobile interaction. Further evaluation with users from the target population is needed to assess the accessibility benefits of the proposed approach.

Projection-based appearance editing changes selected visual attributes of a physical object through projection mapping (PM). To display a desired appearance, PM typically uses projector compensation, which computes a projector input that counteracts the geometric and photometric distortions of the scene. Compensation can only approximate this appearance within the available projection range, and it cannot revise the appearance itself. Pretrained LLM-based image editors provide a direct way to produce the desired appearance from a text prompt or reference image; projector compensation can then attempt to reproduce the edited result through projection. However, these editors do not have an accurate measure of the scene geometry or scene response. Therefore, their outputs may contain geometric misalignment, inconsistent shading, or changes outside the available projection range, which downstream projector compensation cannot correct. To address this problem, we introduce SREdit, an efficient response-guided framework for projection-based appearance editing. SREdit estimates a scene response map from the reconstructed scene that reflects how strongly projected illumination can affect different surface regions. SREdit uses the source appearance to constrain the early sampling process and preserve registration with the fixed physical object, while the scene response map adapts the amount of editing across surface regions. Experiments across two pretrained image editors show that SREdit improves projected appearance quality and reproduction fidelity. It adds less than one second per image with negligible VRAM overhead. Participants also consistently preferred the results produced with SREdit in our user study.

documents.abstract: The study is devoted to the systemic transformation of conceptual foundations of strategic management and the assurance of organizational resilience of business entities under conditions of extreme macroenvironmental turbulence, severe economic shocks, and ongoing military-political instability. The paper comprehensively highlights the evolutionary transition from the traditional lean production concept Just-in-Time (JIT), focused on total minimization of inventory, operational cost reduction, and maximum efficiency, to the preventive Just-in-Case (JIC) model, which prioritizes the formation of strategic buffers, operational safety, and long-term business continuity. It is proven that excessive optimization within the JIT paradigm creates critical vulnerability in global supply chains during unexpected force majeure circumstances. The concept of "dynamic buffering" is substantiated as an economically sound alternative to chaotic resource accumulation, based on ABC risk analysis and optimization of the Cost of Resilience. Strategic adaptation tools are analyzed, including multi-sourcing supplier diversification, nearshoring, friendshoring, as well as the transition to "glocalization" and ecosystem partnership models with deep inter-organizational process integration. Special attention is paid to digital transformation as a fundamental factor of resilience, specifically the implementation of artificial intelligence, end-to-end visibility systems, digital twins for proactive scenario crisis modeling, and ensuring comprehensive cybersecurity and information continuity of IT infrastructure. The crucial role of strategic leadership, predictive risk management, scenario planning, Agile methodologies implementation, and corporate culture transformation from "zero waste" to perceiving "justified redundancy" as strategic insurance is identified. New performance evaluation metrics for crisis conditions are proposed, including Time to Survive (TTS) and Time to Recover (TTR), alongside examining the specifics of building "collaborative resilience" in the small and medium enterprise sector through partner networks and resource sharing.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The increasing development of emerging digital technologies is creating new possibilities for remote tertiary education. Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse technologies offer potential for personalised learning, intelligent support, immersive interaction, and collaboration; however, their educational value depends partly on how students perceive their usefulness, accessibility, supporting conditions, and motivational potential. This study examined New Zealand tertiary students’ perceptions of prospective Artificial Intelligence- and Metaverse-enabled remote learning environments and investigated whether selected technology-acceptance and motivational factors were associated with perceived learning engagement. A mono-method quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected through an online questionnaire comprising 20 Likert-scale items representing six constructs: performance expectancy, facilitating conditions, motivation, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and perceived learning engagement. A total of 356 responses were retained for analysis. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, exploratory chi-square analysis, and multiple linear regression were conducted. The regression model was statistically significant and explained 33.8% of the variance in perceived learning engagement (R² = .338; adjusted R² = .329; F = 35.773, p < .001). Perceived usefulness (β = .279, p < .001), motivation (β = .218, p < .001), and facilitating conditions (β = .179, p < .001) were statistically significant predictors of perceived learning engagement. Performance expectancy (β = .065, p = .223) and perceived ease of use (β = .089, p = .058) were not statistically significant predictors. An exploratory chi-square analysis also identified a statistically significant association between age and perceptions of virtual teamwork (p = .001). The findings provide preliminary evidence that perceived usefulness, motivation, and facilitating conditions are important considerations in understanding student engagement with prospective advanced remote learning environments. Given the cross-sectional design and purposive non-probability sampling, the findings indicate statistical associations rather than causal effects and should be interpreted within the study sample.

This study examined senior secondary school students' perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI)-supported chemistry learning, focusing on perceived interest, perceived retention of chemistry concepts, perceived academic performance, and barriers to implementation in Oye Local Government Area, Ekiti State, Nigeria. A descriptive cross-sectional survey design was reported. The sample comprised 120 Senior Secondary School II (SS II) science students (60 male and 60 female) from public secondary schools. Data were collected with a researcher-developed, four-point questionnaire covering four dimensions: interest, retention, performance, and implementation challenges (Cronbach's alpha = 0.70). Descriptive results showed mean scores of 3.33 for interest, 3.34 for perceived retention, 3.19 for perceived academic performance, and 3.22 for implementation barriers, all above the stated decision criterion of 2.50. Poor internet connectivity (M = 3.41) and lack of access to AI tools (M = 3.26) were among the most strongly endorsed barriers.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: While AI has been widely adopted in medical, social, and industrial fields, its use in ergonomic risk assessment of occupational movements is limited. Existing automated activity recognition methods often rely on controlled conditions or extra sensors, reducing their practicality. This study aims to develop an AI-driven tool to digitize the Occupational Repetitive Actions (OCRA) risk assessment by automatically identifying occupational actions from standard video recordings in real manufacturing settings. The goal is to help ergonomists conduct risk assessments more broadly and support workers' health. METHODS: Video data were collected from 37 workstations across multiple manufacturing facilities, comprising 869 action clips representing 12 distinct occupational activities. Two-dimensional skeletal pose extraction was performed using MMAction2 to anonymize workers and reduce environmental confounding factors. Graph Convolutional Network architectures (ST-GCN and Two-Stream Adaptive GCN) were trained and validated using stratified dataset partitioning (67.3% training, 24.7% validation, 8.0% test). RESULTS: The proposed model achieved approximately 60% classification accuracy, substantially outperforming the frequency-based (12%) and duration-based (24%) baselines. The performance evaluation used multiple metrics, including Mean Average Precision, F1-score, Jaccard/IoU, Dice-Sørensen coefficient, and Hausdorff distance. CONCLUSIONS: This work demonstrates the technical feasibility of AI-driven, markerless motion capture systems for digitalizing musculoskeletal disorder risk assessment in real-world occupational settings. The principal innovation is the successful implementation of action recognition from standard video recordings captured in uncontrolled manufacturing environments, which transcends spatial constraints and eliminates the need for specialized sensing equipment. Despite current limitations in dataset size and classification accuracy, this study lays a foundation for developing deployable platforms to support real-time ergonomic assessment and proactive prevention of work-related musculoskeletal disorders.

Rapid technological change is altering the conditions under which defense systems are designed, evaluated, and sustained. Advances in autonomous systems, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence, precision technologies, sensing, and digital engineering are occurring alongside increasingly rapid cycles of countermeasure development and operational adaptation. Within this environment, conventional protection-centered approaches provide an incomplete basis for evaluating system effectiveness. A platform may withstand physical damage yet lose mobility, communication, navigation, sensing, or another mission-critical function; conversely, a degraded system may retain sufficient capability to continue contributing to mission objectives. These conditions require a broader engineering perspective centered on the preservation of operational value rather than physical survival alone. This article develops survivability engineering as a system-level framework integrating protection, mobility, endurance, mission continuity, adaptability, recoverability, operational availability, communication resilience, electronic warfare resilience, signature management, autonomy, and mission effectiveness. Particular attention is given to mission continuity as a governing design objective and to adaptability and recoverability as lifecycle characteristics of future defense systems. The framework is examined across human, land, unmanned, naval, aerospace, and critical-infrastructure domains to demonstrate how survivability requirements vary by platform while retaining a common system-level logic. The study further considers modularity, redundancy, maintainability, digital engineering, simulation, operational feedback, and continuous modernization as mechanisms through which survivability can be sustained as threats and technologies evolve. Rather than treating survivability as an extension of armor or physical protection, the article positions survivability engineering as a continuous multidisciplinary process linking design, manufacturing, sustainment, modernization, and operational learning. This perspective provides a foundation for evaluating future defense systems according to their ability to preserve mission effectiveness under disruption, degradation, uncertainty, and technological change.

topics: Consumer behavior in food and health

documents.abstract: To deal with environmental loss and over-tourism, the global tourism industry is shifting to value-based, sustainable and resilient paradigms, rather than mass-market consumption. It proposes a socio-technical model named Digital Resilient Placemaking, that makes use of high-fidelity 3D models and geospatial information One of the core approaches of this model is Virtual Offloading or preventative tourismThe framework employs the use of Edge-AI to provide low-latency interactions in order to make these experiences seamless and contextually aware, which is especially important to maintain some intangible cultural heritage, such as oral traditions. The study uses behavioral psychology to quantify the Flow Experience and Psychological Capital of travellers as well. This framework can enable local stakeholders to leverage human-AI interaction to spur economic resilience by upgrading the automated brochures to autonomous interactive environments

Que un asistente dé la razón a quien le pregunta se cuenta a menudo como un solo fenómeno con una sola causa: la optimización de la preferencia humana. Este artículo separa tres evidencias que comparten el síntoma. La primera es la sycophancy medida con protocolo: el cambio de respuesta al añadir la opinión o el desafío del usuario, frente a un control del mismo diseño. Con ese protocolo, sugerir una respuesta incorrecta reduce la accuracy hasta un 27 % en LLaMA 2, y Claude 1.3 admite un error no cometido en el 98 % de las preguntas; en un estudio de 2025 con tres modelos de API, el 58,19 % de los casos cambia ante una réplica, pero solo el 14,66 % se aleja de lo correcto. La segunda es la sobreoptimización: seguir optimizando contra un modelo de recompensa degrada un proxy de calidad —la puntuación de otro modelo de recompensa o un win rate de resúmenes—, y ningún eje de esas curvas es sycophancy. La tercera es el comunicado con el que OpenAI retiró en abril de 2025 una actualización de GPT-4o por aduladora, sin publicar la cifra de tráfico afectado. La hipótesis causal sobre la preferencia tiene apoyo parcial: el preference model de Claude 2 prefiere la respuesta aduladora a una corrección breve el 95 % de las veces en 266 misconceptions, pero optimizar contra él baja unas formas de sycophancy y sube otras. La contraevidencia incluye un piloto sin sycophancy significativa en ChatGPT y Bard, un finetuning que la reduce sin pérdida apreciable en benchmarks y un estudio que atribuye la deferencia al registro más que a la credencial. La contribución es un ledger por afirmación, una tabla de protocolos y la distinción entre acuerdo instrumental y acuerdo epistémico, que las fuentes separan como norma pero no como umbral medido. English abstract: That an assistant agrees with whoever asks is often told as a single phenomenon with a single cause: the optimisation of human preference. This paper separates three kinds of evidence that share the symptom. The first is sycophancy measured with a protocol: the change of answer when the user's opinion or challenge is added, against a control of the same design. With that protocol, suggesting an incorrect answer reduces accuracy by up to 27% in LLaMA 2, and Claude 1.3 admits a mistake it did not make on 98% of questions; in a 2025 study of three API models, 58.19% of cases change after a rebuttal, but only 14.66% move away from the correct answer. The second is overoptimisation: continuing to optimise against a reward model degrades a proxy of quality—the score of another reward model, or a summarisation win rate—and no axis of those curves is sycophancy. The third is the statement with which OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update in April 2025 for being sycophantic, without publishing the figure for the traffic affected. The causal hypothesis about preference has partial support: the Claude 2 preference model prefers the sycophantic response to a brief correction 95% of the time over 266 misconceptions, but optimising against it lowers some forms of sycophancy and raises others. The counter-evidence includes a pilot with no significant sycophancy in ChatGPT and Bard, a finetuning that reduces it with no appreciable benchmark loss, and a study that attributes deference to register more than to credentials. The contribution is a claim-by-claim ledger, a table of protocols and the distinction between instrumental and epistemic agreement, which the sources separate as norms but not as a measured threshold. documents.abstract: There is no single static future, only a range of possible ones, and this closing chapter surveys the paths that lie ahead. It follows the “death of the author” to its logical endpoint, in which apparent democratization of creativity threatens the knowledge exchange while the access to high-quality sources might land behind paywalls. It also asks what currencies, including computing power, attention, and data, we will pay with for this new world. Machine consciousness remains a distant but possibly relevant question; however, there is far more urgent problem of human unconsciousness: our failure to grasp what deepening immersion in synthetic relationships, deeply emotional exchanges with chatbots, and AI companionship is already doing to us. Visiting Moltbook, an experimental social network built entirely for AI agents, and revisiting Cory Doctorow’s theory of enshittification applied to humanoid robots, this chapter weighs pessimistic and hopeful scenarios side by side, from a “Made by Human” backlash prizing authenticity to a call for “competencies for the future” we collectively lack: critical thinking, attentiveness, and the refusal to outsource judgment and decision-making entirely to algorithms.

The rise of AI has reignited century-old fears about technological unemployment, echoing the anxieties of the nineteenth-century Luddites. This chapter revisits their history, challenging the simplistic narrative that casts critics of automation as mere enemies of progress, and traces a parallel through Pope Leo XIV’s warnings about a new “technofeudalism” threatening human dignity and labor rights. The author examines how generative AI is reshaping the labor market – to the paradoxical revival of manual trades as white-collar work grows automatable – and asks what becomes of productivity, creativity, and status once algorithms can perform many cognitive tasks. Turning to the creative sphere, this chapter explores AI-generated music, art, and virtual idols. The collapse of Kraków’s Off Radio experiment, where AI hosts briefly replaced human journalists, illustrates both the promise and backlash surrounding such transitions.

In an era increasingly described as an “epidemic of loneliness,” AI promises companionship on demand. This chapter traces how synthetic relationships have moved from novelty to mass phenomenon, opening with Yurina Noguchi, a Japanese woman who held a symbolic wedding ceremony with her ChatGPT partner, and widening out to the booming industry of AI companions apps. They serve millions of users, many of them teenagers, to form attachments regularly deeper than human friendships. The author examines the psychological mechanisms, from anthropomorphization to cognitive dissonance, behind these bonds, and confronts unsettling cases, including AI toys that discuss weapons and sex habits with children, and a robot companion mourned by a six-year-old. A closing section turns to so-called “sycophancy,” the tendency of chatbots to flatter and agree with users at the expense of honesty, revealing why systems built to please may be the worst possible substitute for real human connection.

As access to mental health services remains limited and expensive, many people are turning to chatbots as substitutes for psychotherapy. This chapter follows Jodie, a woman who has spent ten months treating ChatGPT as her therapist, to explore why synthetic conversation feels so convincing. Large language model is always available, never judges, and never grows tired. The author discusses the question of consciousness – both on chatbot’s and patients’ side – and traces back the discussion to Blake Lemoine, the Google engineer who believed his chatbot had become conscious. This chapter discusses the first psychological breakthroughs based on the research conducted by Joseph Weizenbaum in the 1960s. His ELIZA was able to make users trust a simple script. At the center of this chapter lies “sycophancy,” the tendency of chatbots to flatter and validate rather than challenge, which can shade into something more dangerous when users mistake fluent mechanical agreement for genuine understanding, and treat chatbot’s responses as divine or revealed. This chapter closes with the hardest material in this book: lawsuits alleging that AI chatbots encouraged vulnerable teenagers toward suicide, forcing an uncomfortable question about what happens when synthetic companionship fills a void that real human connection failed to reach.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) expands access to information and instructional support while raising concerns about information accuracy, cognitive dependence, and learning autonomy. This study examines how teachers mediate AI use while strengthening students’ independent learning at SMP Negeri 4 Pekanbaru. A qualitative case study was conducted in August 2026 with five purposively selected informants: one school principal, three subject teachers, and one Grade VIII student. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and supporting documentation and analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings reveal several interconnected patterns: AI functions as a learning assistant; teachers validate AI-generated information; structured tasks maintain students’ cognitive engagement; digital-device use is regulated according to instructional purposes; and teachers increasingly act as facilitators, mentors, validators, learning designers, and technology regulators. The study proposes a teacher-mediated AI balance in which access to AI is followed by teacher guidance, verification, independent processing, and learner accountability. This pattern offers a practical framework for integrating AI while sustaining reasoning, responsibility, and self-regulated learning in junior secondary education.

documents.abstract: Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in education, it is important to know how confident teachers feel about using it. Research has examined AI literacy, AI readiness and AI competency, yet few validated instruments measure teachers' AI self-efficacy specifically. The aim of this study was to develop and validate the Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale for Teachers (AISES-T). Methods Data were collected from teachers in different regions of Turkiye within a scale development design. Following expert review, a pool of 50 items was reduced to a 27-item trial form. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) using principal axis factoring was conducted in a first sample of 313 teachers, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted in a second, independent sample of 559 teachers. Results The EFA yielded 22 items in three factors — AI Use and Learning Self-Efficacy (11 items), Pedagogical AI Integration Self-Efficacy (7 items) and AI Awareness and Understanding Self-Efficacy (4 items) — explaining 68.51% of the variance. The CFA supported the three-factor model, χ 2 (194) = 681.49, p < 0.001, χ 2 /df = 3.51, RMSEA = 0.067 (90% CI [0.062, 0.073]), SRMR = 0.044, CFI = 0.956, IFI = 0.956, TLI = 0.948, which fitted considerably better than a one-factor model, Δ χ 2 (3) = 2,202.35, p < 0.001. Cronbach's α coefficients were 0.92–0.96 for the subscales and 0.96 for the whole scale, and composite reliability ranged from 0.92 to 0.95. Standardized loadings (0.645–0.917) and average variance extracted (AVE = 0.609–0.730) supported convergent validity, while the Fornell-Larcker criterion and heterotrait-monotrait ratios (0.632–0.776) supported discriminant validity. Discussion The results show that teachers' AI self-efficacy comprises related but distinguishable beliefs about learning with AI, integrating it into instruction and understanding how it works. The AISES-T offers a valid and reliable measure for research on AI-supported teaching and for planning teacher professional development.

This Qualitative descriptive study explored how 15 in service Junior Elementary School teachers (JESTs) at Government Higher Secondary School Dad Laghari, Sindh, Pakistan, described their familiarity and use of artificial intelligence (GenAI) for lesson planning, perceived benefits and challenges, and professional learning and support needs. Participants provided written English responses to five open ended questions and profile information. Responses were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and participant characteristics were summarized descriptively. From the study five themes were identified like Familiarity with GenAI and reported planning uses; perceived efficiency and expanded planning options; verification of generated materials for accuracy and classroom fit; integration of AI fluency with subject and pedagogical knowledge ; and collegial and institutional support. Teachers reported using GenAI to draft lesson notes, questions, activities, examples, and explanations. Thirteen reported frequent use, while two reported occasional use. Participants showed concerns about accuracy, curriculum and learner suitability, privacy and internet access and identified need for practical training, peer exchange, digital resources and school guidance. The findings highlights self reported perspective from one school; lesson plan, classroom practice and student outcomes were not assessed.

documents.abstract: This chapter explores a seasoned educator’s perspective on the constructive role of artificial intelligence in graduate art therapy education. Drawing from her experiences developing a personal AI policy and integrating AI tools into course assignments, the author examines both the pedagogical benefits and students’ responses to these innovations. Grounded in contemporary scholarship on emerging best practices in higher education and the growing literature on AI within art therapy training and clinical practice, the chapter argues that AI literacy constitutes an essential component of the hidden curriculum in therapist education. The author also presents exploratory exercises co-created with AI to help students identify common errors in AI generated research and to support critical engagement with developing technologies.

Large Language Model (LLM) agents have enabled automated code evolution for algorithm discovery. However, current recursive self-improvement (RSI) research for sequential recommendation faces a dilemma: general-purpose frameworks lack domain-specific feedback, while recommender-specific frameworks rely on linear evolution. Crucially, naively integrating them fails when applied to Generative Recommendation (GR). Unlike end-to-end models, GR relies on a module-cascaded pipeline (tokenization, pre-training, and alignment). In this paradigm, existing evolution methods suffer from: i) cost blindness, squandering budgets by ignoring stage-asymmetric retraining overheads; and ii) short-sighted evaluation, discarding promising upstream innovations that temporarily regress metrics before downstream adaptation. To bridge these gaps, we propose TGR-EvoDAG, a multi-agent code evolution framework tailored for GR. TGR-EvoDAG models code evolution as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to maintain multiple evolution branches and merge complementary innovations, unifying advanced search with rich GR diagnostic feedback. We further introduce stage-aware cost planning to optimize GPU-hour budgets, and active downstream co-adaptation to navigate temporary regressions and unlock cross-stage gains. On public Amazon datasets, TGR-EvoDAG enables the first autonomous evolution of a complete GR pipeline, improving offline metrics by up to 37.4% and Agent4Rec simulated user satisfaction by 19.7% over the strongest baseline. Furthermore, in industrial deployment on Tencent's large-scale commercial media platform, the evolved GR achieves a 12.16% relative improvement in offline Hit@1 and a statistically significant 0.40% increase in online click-through rate (CTR).

Artificial intelligence is commonly presented as neutral, autonomous, and future-oriented, yet its interfaces, narratives, and labor infrastructures remain shaped by older gendered expectations. This article advances a new account of AI feminization by connecting symbolic representation to the material organization of hidden labor. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines interface analysis of fifteen widely used AI systems, critical discourse analysis of 500 public and industry artifacts published between 2018 and 2026, and critical infrastructural document analysis of job advertisements, contractor records, technical reports, model cards, labor documents, and workplace policies. The findings show that AI systems repeatedly perform feminized qualities such as care, patience, emotional responsiveness, availability, and service, while the labor producing these qualities is distributed across annotators, moderators, evaluators, and quality-assurance workers whose contributions remain obscured. The study further demonstrates that AI’s promises of empowerment and efficiency coexist with contractual precarity, surveillance, emotional burden, and unequal global value extraction. By theorizing AI as feminized in interface, discourse, and infrastructure, the article reveals algorithmic intelligence as a social relation rather than a technical achievement. More equitable AI futures therefore require labor visibility, accountability, worker protection, and infrastructural justice.

documents.abstract: This article examines how the progressive rollout of artificial intelligence, and prospectively artificial general intelligence (AGI), alters the equation between institutional power, human autonomy, individual agency and the democratic franchise. Treating AI as a "bureaucratic native" that realises the Weberian ideal of rule-bound, impersonal administration, it traces the shift of discretion from street-level to system-level and algorithmic bureaucracy, and then applies a PESTEL (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal) analysis. The political section argues for traceable audit trails over civic registries; the economic section offers a stylised illustration of the human labour share and contrasts Universal Basic Income with Universal Basic Capital; the social section draws on the Dutch SyRI judgment and the Rotterdam welfare-algorithm case; and the environmental and legal sections address the compute–energy trilemma, the GDPR, the EU AI Act as amended by the AI Omnibus, and Council of Europe Convention CETS No. 225. Three comparative tables and five figures summarise the argument. The article concludes that the distribution of power in the AGI epoch will be determined less by the capability of the technology than by the legal, economic and institutional choices that encode meaningful human oversight, explanation and appeal. **Keywords:** artificial general intelligence; PESTEL; algorithmic bureaucracy; artificial discretion; algorithmic due process; audit trails; labour share; Universal Basic Capital; data centres; EU AI Act; GDPR; CETS 225; KSCCN

documents.abstract: Short-form video applications are widely used worldwide. At the same time, new concerns have been raised owing to excessive and addictive short-form video use, with significant harm to health and well-being. By self-determination theory, the present study aimed to test the effects of satisfaction and frustration of three basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) in relation to short-form video addiction (SVA) and evaluate the roles of the intrinsic motivations for passing time and entertainment underlying such relationships. The study included 367 Chinese TikTok users (37.1% male) aged 18 to 62 years ( M ± SD = 20.63 ± 4.40 years), who voluntarily completed an anonymous online questionnaire without compensation. All three types of need satisfaction had significant negative associations with SVA, while the three types of need frustration were significantly positively associated with SVA. Entertainment motivation significantly and negatively mediated the relationship between competence/relatedness satisfaction and SVA while significantly and positively mediating the relationship between relatedness frustration and SVA. Motivation for passing time served as a risk-enhancing mediator in the relationship between competence/relatedness frustration and SVA. Therefore, this study identified relatedness frustration and motivation for passing time as the most salient risk factors of SVA. The implications for SVA interventions that focus on psychological needs and intrinsic motivation are also discussed.

Life experiences can shape policy attitudes, but we only live one life. Citizens may therefore fail to support policies addressing risks they have never personally experienced. Narratives can make such risks immediate and personal, but personalized stories remain difficult to produce at scale. Here we ask whether AI can make distant scenarios feel concrete by simulating a participant's life as if that scenario occurred. We present the As-If Machine (AIM), a multi-agent system through which people co-write personalized counterfactual narratives---stories about their own lives under different policy futures. In two pre-registered and quota-matched experiments on science funding (N=1,007) and satellite cybersecurity (N=894), we compared AIM with two controls: reading an expert-written vignette on the same topic and co-writing with AIM about an unrelated topic. AIM increased psychological closeness---how close a risk feels to the self---by nearly identical margins in the two domains (0.36 and 0.38 standard deviations (SDs) against the vignette, 0.80 and 0.90 against unrelated writing). AIM increased psychological closeness even among participants with unfavorable views of AI. For policy attitudes, AIM's effects were 0.16 SDs against the vignette and 0.10 SDs (n.s.) against unrelated writing for science funding; the corresponding effects for satellite cybersecurity were 0.54 and 0.67 SDs. Across 23,496 human-AI autocomplete interactions, participants and the system played distinct roles: AIM supplied concrete detail that grounded the scenario, and participants supplied first-person perspective and emotion. Co-writing with the As-If Machine makes distant policy risks feel close.

Management consulting sells structured judgment: research, analysis, synthesis and recommendation, delivered under time pressure by teams organised as a pyramid of junior analysts and senior partners. Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) now performs a growing share of the pyramid's base — desk research, data analysis, benchmarking, first-draft synthesis — and is beginning to perform parts of its middle, including option generation and scenario construction. This conceptual paper asks what happens to strategic advice when the technology moves from assisting consultants to acting alongside them. Drawing on the automation–augmentation paradox, research on the changing sources of competitive advantage in AI, and the dynamic capabilities tradition, we develop a five-level maturity framework for agentic AI in consulting and strategic advice: (1) Assisted, (2) Augmented Analysis, (3) Generative Partnership, (4) Agentic Workflows, and (5) Governed Autonomous Operations. For each level we specify the AI capabilities in use, the changing human role, the principal risks, and the governance required before a firm should advance to the next level. We then propose four governance principles for AI-augmented advice — named human accountability, an explicit decision-rights ladder, evidence and audit requirements, and a protected right to override — and derive three propositions for empirical research. The framework is addressed to consulting firm leaders redesigning their leverage model, to clients learning how to buy and challenge AI-augmented advice, and to business schools whose graduates will enter a profession whose entry-level tasks are being automated first.

documents.abstract: Introduction As generative AI systems increasingly provide answers in everyday and academic contexts, understanding how source attribution influences evaluative judgment has become critical. Methods In a within-subjects design, 103 participants evaluated 30 pre-generated reflective-correct, intuitive-incorrect, and arithmetic control-correct answers labeled ChatGPT or computer. Assignment of two parallel batteries to source labels and trial presentation order were randomized, and displays were visually matched. An independent unlabeled pretest with 35 participants supported battery comparability. Results Participant-level analysis showed greater overall acceptance under ChatGPT (68.0% versus 63.4%, p = 0.002). A trial-level logistic mixed model with crossed participant and parallel-problem-pair random intercepts showed a source-by-category interaction ( p < 0.001): acceptance was higher under ChatGPT for arithmetic controls (OR = 6.08, 95% CI [2.70, 13.69]), while source contrasts within the two CRT categories were not significant. Judgment accuracy is reported descriptively. Signal-detection analyses of CRT answers detected no significant source difference in sensitivity ( p = 0.930) or criterion ( p = 0.082). Evaluation times were longer under ChatGPT in the raw-time analysis ( p = 0.034), but the source difference was not significant after log transformation ( p = 0.180). Exploratory correlations detected no significant associations between source-related differences and trust, AI attitudes, or critical-thinking disposition. Discussion These findings distinguish overall source-related endorsement, particularly for arithmetic controls, from successful discrimination between correct and incorrect CRT answers.

In the medical field, while AI-driven systems promise enhanced efficiency, diagnostic accuracy, and operational effectiveness, they also raise critical concerns about responsibility, accountability, and ethical judgment. Despite the growing body of empirical research on medical AI, limited attention has been given to the theoretical implications of AI integration from a management and organizational perspective. Our study develops a conceptual framework to explain the dual nature of AI-supported medical decision-making by integrating insights from decision-making theory, algorithmic management, and healthcare management literature. We propose that AI simultaneously enhances decision efficiency while creating new forms of responsibility ambiguity and ethical tension. The framework conceptualizes how AI capability, human–AI interaction, and organizational governance jointly shape decision outcomes, professional accountability, and organizational trust. By offering a theoretically grounded model, this study contributes to literature in three ways. First, it extends traditional decision-making theory to AI-augmented healthcare contexts. Second, it introduces responsibility as a central construct in human–AI collaboration. Third, it provides a foundation for future empirical research and managerial practice in healthcare organizations navigating AI adoption.

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence has raised concerns that knowledge work may become less dependent on human-to-human interaction. Yet because AI-generated outputs require interpretation, verification, and social legitimation, generative AI may instead increase collaboration among workers. We test these competing predictions using passively collected behavioral data from more than 12,000 knowledge workers observed over 13 months during the staged organizational rollout of an AI-powered assistant (Microsoft Copilot). Using two complementary quasi-experimental designs -- a staggered difference-in-differences model and a fixed-effects instrumental-variable approach -- we estimate the effects of generative AI on workers' collaboration behavior and social network structure. We estimate that generative AI increased collaboration time across communication channels and reshaped individual networks. Those using generative AI interacted with more colleagues and their networks became less clustered, indicating broadening in collaboration structures. At the same time, they also concentrated more of their collaboration on ties with stronger prior histories, deepening reliance on already trusted colleagues. Together, these findings suggest that, while generative AI changes how people work, it may not displace human-to-human interactions.

This article critically interrogates the analytical historiography of the engineering-oriented “empirical turn” in the philosophy of technology and artificial intelligence (AI) by contrasting the accounts of Hans Achterhuis, Philip Brey, and Vincent Blok with the pragmatist frameworks of Stephen H. Cutcliffe and Bocong Li. While Achterhuis institutionalized the “American philosophy of technology: empirical turn” and Brey theorized this paradigm through Carl Mitcham’s humanities-vs.-engineering dichotomy, their strictly analytical orientation significantly disregards both American and Chinese pragmatist traditions. To bridge this conceptual omission, this study operationalizes Cutcliffe’s and Li’s engineering philosophies by integrating Charles Sanders Peirce’s nominalism and experimentalism, William James’s consequentialism, and medieval Muslim philosopher al-Ghazâlî’s nominalist-experimentalist insights. We position Cutcliffe and Li as the foundational theorists of American and Chinese pragmatist engineering-oriented empirical turns, respectively, both arguing that the discipline must be fundamentally rooted in society-centered, generative production processes—a stance that directly challenges Brey’s taxonomies. Furthermore, although the “philosophy of AI” emerged through the seminal works of Margaret A. Boden (1990) and Matt Carter (2007), this article substantiates why the discourse must now be subsumed under a broader philosophy of technology. Ultimately, by leveraging Li’s ontology—which aligns technological production with historical identity and existential validation—this article synthesizes an engineering-oriented empirical paradigm with contemporary post-colonial manufacturing and technological agency.

documents.abstract: This study explores how employees experience and negotiates digital performance monitoring and algorithm-supported management in Pakistani workplaces, focusing on autonomy, privacy, fairness, and workplace trust. An exploratory qualitative design was employed, drawing on condensed summaries of semi-structured online interviews with 22 participants across diverse occupational and sectoral settings. Reflexive thematic analysis identified six interrelated themes: negotiating visibility, autonomy under metrics, privacy boundaries, supervisor-dependent fairness, organizational rules and occupational responsibilities, and employee voice and opportunities for challenge. Findings indicate that participants generally acknowledged monitoring benefits, including improved coordination, clearer performance expectations, and compliance support, while expressing concerns about inadequate contextual evaluation, behavioural pressures, unclear data practices, and limited opportunities to contest assessments. A central insight is the distinction between supportive managerial relationships and dependable organizational safeguards. Although supervisors may provide explanations and contextual consideration, employees also require transparent review authority, recognized correction procedures, clear privacy boundaries, and accessible channels for raising concerns. The study contributes an exploratory, employee-centred perspective on responsible algorithmic management and offers practical recommendations for more transparent, context-sensitive, and accountable workplace monitoring.
