documents.abstract: AbstractObjective: This study aimed to identify the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, specifically machine learning, natural language processing, intelligent robots, and decision support systems, on the work environment of organizations operating in Riyadh.Methodology: The study employed a descriptive-analytical approach. The study population consisted of employees working in organizations implementing AI technologies in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. A simple random sample of 394 employees was used, and an electronic questionnaire was the primary data collection tool.Results: The study found a high level of AI technology implementation in Riyadh organizations, with a mean score of 4.06. The quality of the work environment was also found to be high, with a mean score of 4.01. A statistically significant effect of AI technologies on the work environment was found at the 0.01 level, with the dimensions collectively explaining 70.8% of the variance in the dependent variable. The "decision support systems" dimension demonstrated the greatest impact.Recommendations: The study recommended enhancing investment in digital infrastructure, designing specialized training programs, expanding the application of decision support systems, and establishing a legislative and ethical framework that regulates the use of these technologies in work environments.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: AbstractObjective: The study aimed to reveal the impact of using Geographic Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) applications on the efficiency of executive decision-making in the National Water Company’s projects in the southern region, through studying four main dimensions: collection and processing of smart spatial data, predictive spatial analysis, spatial visualization and decision support, and operational integration with project management. The study also examined the extent to which these applications reflect on the quality of decisions made and the speed of response to problems related to implementation.Methodology: The study followed the descriptive analytical approach. The study population consisted of employees related to the fields of operation and maintenance, digital transformation, and geographic information systems, in addition to employees in the administrative and technical fields of the company under study. The purposive sampling method was followed, and the study sample amounted to (34) employees from the National Water Company in the Southern Region. The questionnaire was used as the primary tool for collecting data.Results: The results showed that the level of use of geographic artificial intelligence applications was very high, with an arithmetic mean of (4.39). The efficiency of executive decision-making was also very high, with an average of (4.47). The average quality of decision and executive response was (4.62). The results proved the existence of a strong and statistically significant positive relationship between the use of GeoAI applications and the efficiency of executive decision-making. It was shown that there was a statistically significant effect of geographic artificial intelligence (GeoAI) applications on the efficiency of executive decision-making in the projects of the National Water Company in the Southern Region, as the applications explained about (79.7%) of the variance in decision efficiency.Recommendations: The study recommended expanding the use of predictive spatial analysis, developing a unified spatial platform, enhancing integration between GeoAI and project management, operation and maintenance systems, along with training staff and establishing a clear framework for data governance and intelligent models.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: AbstractObjective: This study aimed to identify the impact of healthcare cost management in its four dimensions (cost planning, cost control, cost analysis, and cost reduction) on operational efficiency in diagnostic radiology departments in public hospitals in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Methodology: The study adopted the descriptive analytical approach. The study population consisted of all employees in the financial, accounting, administrative and technical departments associated with the diagnostic radiology departments in the public hospitals affiliated with the Ministry of Health in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The simple random sampling method was adopted, and the questionnaire tool was adopted, as it was distributed to (380) individuals from the employees in the financial, accounting and technical departments associated with the radiology departments in the public hospitals in the five main administrative regions of the Kingdom. (328) questionnaires were returned that were valid for statistical analysis at a rate of (86.32%).Results: The study found a substantial and direct relationship between health cost management and operational efficiency in diagnostic radiology departments in public hospitals in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, positive and statistically significant at the level of (0.01). It also showed a statistically significant positive effect at the significance level of (0.05) of health cost management with its combined dimensions on operational efficiency, as the coefficient of determination reached a value of (0.709), meaning that the dimensions of cost management explain (70.9%) of the variance in operational efficiency. The dimensions of health cost management in their impact on operational efficiency were ranked in descending order as follows: cost control, then cost analysis, then cost planning, and finally cost reduction.Recommendations: The study recommended the need to adopt modern methods in cost management such as activity-based costing (ABC) and target costing, employ artificial intelligence techniques and business intelligence tools, enhance cost control through specialized units for analyzing deviations, and develop the quality system in diagnostic radiology departments.

Abstract We study how large language model (LLM) based recommendations affect evaluations of uncertainty. We elicit certainty equivalents for (i) lotteries that share the same reduced-form winning probability but vary in cognitive demands because they are compound, and (ii) an Ellsberg-style ambiguous lottery. Across all lottery types, valuations from participants who receive LLM-based recommendations before each valuation exhibit second-order stochastic dominance relative to valuations from participants who do not. Hence, LLM-based recommendations leave mean valuations unchanged but compress the distribution, reducing the incidence of extreme valuations. Consistent with this pattern, LLM-based recommendations reduce the intensity of risk, complexity, and ambiguity aversion, while leaving the fraction of participants classified as averse unchanged.

This chapter explores the intersection between dark patterns and cybersecurity, highlighting how manipulative interface designs contribute to emerging cyber threats. It outlines key mechanisms through which dark patterns exploit cognitive biases such as urgency, scarcity, and social proof, increasing user susceptibility to social engineering attacks. The chapter examines evolving threat vectors, including phishing, spoofed interfaces, malware delivery, and ClickFix-style attacks, which leverage deceptive user interface (UI) elements. It also discusses the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in amplifying both offensive and defensive cybersecurity strategies. Through analysis of recent threat trends, the chapter emphasizes the growing importance of human factors in security breaches. Finally, it addresses ethical, regulatory, and design-based mitigation strategies, advocating for transparent interfaces, user awareness, and integrated security frameworks to reduce risks and enhance trust in digital systems.

This article argues that instruction-fine-tuned language models should be understood as implementing a genre, what is proposed as the instructional-conversational genre. This genre is an amalgamation of discursive language from prior conversations between generative models and humans recursively run through these massive neural networks. It is instantiated in applications through instruction fine-tuning, the inclusion of a pretext known as a system prompt, and the formalization of inputs in mark-up languages characterized by the use of special tokens and role assignment in turntaking structures.

The article analyzes the leading role of technological factors in the development of the global online education market. The impact of the spread of the Worldwide Web, mobile devices, cloud services, artificial intelligence, e-learning, personalization of learning, virtual and augmented reality, information security, big data, and gamification of learning on the transformation of the educational environment is considered. It is shown that digital technologies have accelerated the transition from traditional forms of education to online formats, expanded access to educational resources, and made learning more flexible, personalized, and scalable. Special attention is paid to how technological innovations are changing the models of interaction between students and educational platforms, improving the quality of content and creating new mechanisms for evaluating learning outcomes. The growth factors of the online education market are also considered, including the development of digital infrastructure, increasing the investment attractiveness of the EdTech sector and the growing demand for distance education services. The paper emphasizes that technological factors are not only a condition, but also the main driver of further expansion of the global online education market. It is concluded that the further development of this field will be determined by the speed of innovation and the ability of educational organizations to adapt to digital transformation.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies

documents.abstract: Large language model agents that use tools could take on part of the electronic health record and desk work that occupies physicians' time, but in many hospitals the medical information systems run inside closed networks, so the model and the agent harness must also be inside the network. We designed, implemented, and deployed LLENS, a clinical support AI agent platform that runs inside the closed network of Hokkaido University Hospital on a single host with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the open-weight model Kimi K2.6 (~1 trillion parameters), and a web application rebuilt from Open WebUI. The harness has 10 components, including page image reading, full-text attachment input, a path-addressed document tree without a vector index, a network-isolated sandbox, artifact return, self-checking of generated output, subagents, and saved procedures. Kimi K2.6 was chosen from 3 open-weight candidates and scored 480/500 on the 2026 Japanese Medical Licensing Examination; it generated 119 tokens/s for a single user and served 16 concurrent requests at 908 tokens/s in total. On 180 questions over hospital documents (3 seeds each), mean accuracy was 10.7% with no documents, 81.3% with fixed retrieval (top 10 chunks of one lexical search), and 97.2% with interactive access, in which the model reads with document tools and the sandbox (15.9 percentage points above fixed retrieval, 95% CI 10.9-21.3); the difference lay in filtering/counting questions (16.7% vs 87.8%). In an automated test of 13 work scenarios (4 runs each), the expected components were triggered in all runs for 12, and 5 scenarios were run with synthetic data on the deployment host. The platform has run on the hospital network since September 14, 2026.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Power systems face climate-driven extremes, compound hazards, rapid electrification and renewable integration, and infrastructure decisions whose consequences persist for decades. These conditions often cannot be represented by historical patterns or well-defined probability distributions. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to forecasting, outage prediction, asset management, optimisation and resilience planning, yet most applications remain prediction-centric, whereas long-horizon grid planning takes place under deep uncertainty. This critical narrative review integrates literature from power-systems engineering, machine learning, climate-risk assessment, infrastructure resilience and decision-making under deep uncertainty to examine how AI can move from forecasting toward robust and adaptive planning. We identify a prediction–planning gap created by two mismatches: a temporal mismatch between the horizons over which AI is predictively competent and those over which infrastructure decisions operate, and an uncertainty mismatch between the stationarity assumptions of learned models and the non-stationary, deeply uncertain conditions of future grids. Distribution shift, rare extremes, model disagreement and optimisation fragility limit prediction-centric approaches. AI offers greater long-term value through scenario exploration, surrogate-accelerated simulation, stress testing, vulnerability discovery, robust multi-objective optimisation and adaptive decision support. We operationalise this shift through an AI-Enabled Adaptive Resilience Planning Framework of six iterative stages, propose a decision-performance evaluation scheme (robustness, regret, adaptability, option value, recovery, equity and tail cost), and set out eight research priorities. Next-generation grid resilience should judge AI not by how accurately it predicts one future, but by how well it supports robust, equitable, explainable and adaptable decisions across many plausible futures.

The Orbital Mind proposes that difficulties of self-regulation can arise from interactions among otherwise useful functions rather than a deficit in one function alone. This paper translates the book's formal research program into a more restricted, testable agenda. A mathematical audit separates properties of a proposed model from consequences that require additional assumptions: mutual inhibition does not guarantee a stable co-active deadlock; a threshold crossing need not be a fold bifurcation; and a generic recurrent network need not possess a scalar potential. A separately specified cubic normal form illustrates conditional predictions about action initiation, cessation and barrier height. Deterministic branch calculations and counterexamples are supplied as reproducible illustrations, not observations of human behavior. Ten hypotheses are organized into staged behavioral, measurement, neural and cross-scale studies. The first priority is a nonclinical action-initiation experiment with parameter and model recovery, matched alternatives, and held-out prediction. No participants, clinical outcomes, fitted psychological parameters or evidence of cross-scale invariance are reported. The contribution is a corrected mathematical specification and a prospective research agenda, not a validated theory of the self. Status: Theoretical and methodological working paper, version 1.0; not peer reviewed. No human participants, clinical results, fitted psychological parameters, preregistration or validation of cross-scale invariance are reported. Materials: The standalone LaTeX PDF is accompanied by the source, deterministic calculation code, 15,606 synthetic equilibrium-branch rows, mathematical checks, environment instructions and checksums. The illustrations do not simulate or validate human behavior. Companion book: The Orbital Mind: The Astrophysics of the Self, by Mayone Maha Rajan, The Maha Research Series, Book 2. Adapted from Part V and Appendices D–F of the October 2026 revised book. Kindle ebook; paperback (ISBN 9798161302286). The book provides conceptual provenance, not evidence validating the proposal. Purchasing the book is not necessary to understand or reproduce the paper. Disclosure: ChatGPT assisted the adaptation, literature checks, mathematical audit, code, drafting and typesetting. The author directs and takes responsibility for the release and has a commercial interest in the companion book. AI assistance is not independent expert review.

This manuscript continues the series on the Yellowstone permutation a (OEIS A098550). Let R(t) be the least odd prime with no multiple among a(1), ..., a(t), for a prime p let n_p be the first index with p | a(n_p), and let E(t) be the number of even terms among a(1), ..., a(t). The previous manuscript of the series proved R(t) <= (2.715 + o(1)) t. We prove that the prime frontier eventually falls behind time: limsup R(t)/t <= 0.9265 < 1, liminf n_p/p >= 1/0.9265 > 1.0793, and liminf E(t)/t >= 0.2440; hence, with the frontier corollary of Part II, a(n) <= max_{j<=n} a(j) <= (0.9265 + o(1)) n ln n. In particular the inequality a(n) <= (pi/2) n ln n of OEIS Conjecture 7 holds for all n >= n_0, where n_0 is ineffective. These constants use a smooth-part Rankin count for the masks, for which two independent proofs are given (Appendices A and B). With Rankin counts only, the same method gives limsup R(t)/t <= 1.045 < pi/2, liminf n_p/p > 0.9569 > 2/pi and liminf E(t)/t >= 0.2301, so liminf n_p/p > 1 is not reached by Rankin counts alone. On the way the manuscript proves the intermediate bounds on limsup R(t)/t: 2.405, 4.625/3, 1.2275, 1.215 and 1.155 (Rankin counts) and 2.14, 4.025/3, 1.1075, 1.08, 2.96/3 and 0.9625 (smooth-part count). The new ingredients are a hole sieve (an even number 2k still unused at time t forces every earlier step with an even anchor and a larger value to have a mask sharing an odd prime with k, by the closure lemma of Part I), the remark that a used odd value above the odd-mask level either has an odd mask or follows an even term, a low chain with a Rankin count at one fixed exponent, few-big-terms rates split by the parity of the mask, an elementary parity count that yields the lower bound on E(t), a split of the forced band at the entry of a prime, and a split of the times into classes according to E(t)/t. All thresholds are ineffective and the results are purely asymptotic; the numerics are double precision with outward-rounded discretisation, not interval arithmetic. Conjecture 7 for all n is NOT proved, no explicit n_0 is given, and a proof of liminf n_p/p >= 1 by Rankin counts alone, as well as the parity bound liminf E(t)/t >= 0.275 used by a conditional result of the program, remain open. AI-assistance and review status: The mathematical content was produced by AI agents (Anthropic Claude) in the author's research program on OEIS A098550, and the text was written by an AI writer agent from the program's internal notes and referee reports. Each section taken from a program note follows a note checked by two independent AI referee agents (separate Claude instances that had not written the text under review), except Appendix A (one full referee report plus two independent re-derivations; the same count has a second, twice-refereed proof in Appendix B); a few lemmas assembled by the writer were checked only by the referees of the assembled text. Each successive assembled version was in addition refereed as a whole by two further AI referees (mathematics; citations, status claims and wording), with all fixes applied; details are in Section 14 of the manuscript. All referee reports cited are AI-generated. No part has been reviewed by a human mathematician. Dependencies: Part I (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23437783), Part II (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23449375), Part III (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23557280) and the previous manuscript on the linear prime frontier (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23558450), and classical results (Rosser-Schoenfeld, Robin, sieve methods as in Halberstam-Richert). One unpublished program result (GIIRG Lemma EV, refereed twice) is used only for the lower bound on R(t)/t and the upper bounds n_p <= (8.197 + o(1)) p and their analogues; the main bounds above do not use it. Conditional statements that rest on further unpublished notes appear only as remarks and are not claimed.

documents.abstract: Health is one of the most fundamental human needs. Ensuring the occupational health and safety of healthcare workers is essential for the safe and effective delivery of healthcare services. This issue has been extensively addressed in graduate theses from various perspectives. To reveal the current state of literature and guide future research, this study examines graduate theses focusing on occupational health and safety in the healthcare sector, in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Accordingly, 555 graduate theses completed between 1990 and 2024 were included in this study were included. The theses included in the study were examined using content analyses. The theses were classified by considering various aspects, such as year of publication, thesis type, university, department, research topic, and research method used. The findings show that most theses were at the master’s level, their number increased steadily over time, and the highest output in the last five years was in 2022. While the theses were produced at 137 different universities, the highest number was produced at Beykent University within the Institute of Health Sciences and the Department of Health Management. Studies focusing on risk assessment and management were the most predominant. The findings of this study are expected to guide and motivate research on occupational health and safety in the healthcare sector.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed the relationship between humans and digital technology. Unlike digital systems that primarily delivered information, mediated interpersonal communication, or provided entertainment, generative AI can respond conversationally, personalise interactions, produce immediate solutions, simulate empathy, reduce cognitive effort, and remain continuously available. These characteristics raise an emerging question: can repeated engagement with generative AI develop into psychologically dependent or addiction-like patterns, and, if so, through what mechanisms? This paper employs an integrative critical literature review and conceptual synthesis to examine problematic generative-AI use through the combined perspectives of behavioural addiction theory, reward and reinforcement processes, the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) model, self-determination theory, compensatory technology use, social anxiety, loneliness, anthropomorphism, cognitive offloading, and human psychological needs. The current study identifies a major gap in the current literature: emerging research frequently examines AI dependence as either a behavioural outcome, an educational problem, or a form of social attachment, but insufficiently integrates the neuropsychological processes of reinforcement with the psychological needs that make generative AI personally rewarding. To address this gap, this paper proposes the Need–Reward–Dependence (NRD) Framework, according to which problematic GenAI engagement develops through the interaction of three processes: unmet or salient psychological needs, rapid need-contingent reinforcement delivered by AI, and repeated cognitive or emotional outsourcing that strengthens habitual reliance. The framework proposes that competence, relatedness, autonomy, reassurance, emotional regulation, cognitive ease, social safety, and control can act as psychologically rewarding affordances of generative AI. Repeated reinforcement may increase cue-reactivity, habitual checking, perceived indispensability, cognitive delegation, emotional attachment, and impaired self-regulation in susceptible users. Importantly, this paper does not claim that generative-AI addiction is currently established as a distinct psychiatric disorder. Rather, it argues that a theoretically coherent and increasingly empirically observable continuum exists from adaptive use through reliance and dependence to potentially compulsive engagement associated with functional impairment. The paper concludes that future research should distinguish productive high-frequency use from clinically meaningful problematic use and should examine the interaction between users’ psychological vulnerabilities and the reward architecture of generative-AI systems
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address a gap in contemporary scholarship on generative artificial intelligence (AI) by shifting attention from the functional evaluation of AI systems to the formative impact of repeated AI use on the human user. It introduces formative evaluation as a complementary approach concerned with how sustained AI use may shape cognitive skills, habits, reasoning, judgment and agency over time. To address this concern, the paper proposes the REAL Framework (Retained, Eroded, Atrophied, Leveraged) as a practical means of evaluating and intentionally shaping patterns of AI use. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual paper develops the REAL Framework through interdisciplinary synthesis and theoretical analysis. It integrates scholarship on human agency and principal-agent relationships with research on cognitive offloading, cognitive reserve, desirable difficulty, automation bias and human–AI collaboration. Emerging empirical research on the cognitive effects of generative AI is used to contextualize and support the framework. The resulting four-dimensional framework is then illustrated through its application to professional practice and considered in relation to potential objections, limitations and directions for future empirical research. Findings The analysis identifies formative evaluation as a distinct and underdeveloped dimension of AI evaluation. While emerging research increasingly documents potential cognitive effects of generative AI use, practical means of evaluating and responding to those effects remain limited. The REAL Framework addresses this gap through four dimensions: Retained, Eroded, Atrophied and Leveraged. Together, these dimensions distinguish between AI use that preserves human agency and cognitive engagement, use that risks over-delegation and capability loss, and use that intentionally leverages AI to enhance human thinking and judgment. Research limitations/implications The REAL Framework is a conceptual and reflective framework that has not yet been empirically validated or operationalized as a measurement instrument. Longitudinal research is needed to examine the formative effects of sustained generative AI use and determine whether structured application of the framework influences patterns of AI delegation or preserves cognitive engagement and capability. Future research should develop and test measures associated with the framework’s four dimensions and examine their applicability across educational, professional and organizational contexts. Practical implications The REAL Framework provides individuals and institutions with a practical means of evaluating how generative AI is being incorporated into learning and professional practice. Its four reflective dimensions can help users identify inappropriate over-delegation, preserve important cognitive and professional capabilities, and redesign AI use to support rather than replace human reasoning and judgment. The framework may also inform institutional guidance, professional development and AI literacy initiatives by shifting attention from whether AI should be used toward how it can be used while preserving meaningful human agency and engagement. Social implications As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in education, work and everyday decision-making, its societal effects will depend not only on the capabilities of AI systems but also on how their use shapes human capabilities over time. The REAL Framework highlights the importance of preserving human agency, reasoning, judgment and cognitive engagement while benefiting from technological advancement. It encourages a broader societal conversation about which human capacities should remain meaningfully exercised and which may appropriately be delegated to increasingly capable AI systems. Originality/value This paper introduces formative evaluation as a distinct conceptual approach to understanding generative AI use, complementing prevailing functional approaches concerned primarily with AI systems, governance and responsible use. It advances the REAL Framework as a structured means of translating emerging concerns about AI’s cognitive and formative effects into reflective practice. By connecting human agency and delegation with cognitive development, the framework shifts attention from evaluating what AI can do to evaluating what repeated AI use may be doing to the human user.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Sociologists face the pressing question of how large language model-based technologies can contribute to social theorising. Several social scientists have called for a greater integration of generative AI tools in the social sciences and humanities to speed and scale up the production of social theory. In this article, we adopt a more cautious approach, reflecting on how the adoption of generative AI raises foundational questions about the construction, refinement and evaluation of critical social theory. To make this argument, we create and critically analyse a speculative piece of dystopian sociological fiction. This enables us to explore the values and practices of critical social theory authorship. We argue that authorship must be ‘recentred’, particularly with regard to four key values of authorial practice: (1) standpoint, (2) creativity, (3) pluralism and (4) accountability. In the present moment, the use of generative AI as substitution for authorial practices redefines and potentially threatens authorship in ways that problematises its particular use in generating critical social theory. With regards to standpoint, generative AI technologies run the risk of reproducing an ‘abstract masculinity’ that feminist scholars have long written against. The relational wonder at the heart of social theory creativity is undermined by generative AI use, as is the pluralism of creativity. Generative AI also flattens and overlooks pluralism of voice, as well as dilutes authorial accountability. We sociologists need to defend and rearticulate what we contribute to social theory and its concomitant politics, both in the theories themselves and in the project of social theorising. It is with this in mind that we call for the ‘rebirth’ - that is, the recentralisation - of the human author in critical social theory creation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: People with intellectual disabilities who experience epilepsy may require additional support for daily activities, seizure monitoring and emergency communication. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and assistive robotics offer opportunities to improve safety and caregiver support. This study reviews the supplied research papers on automated seizure detection, AI-based epilepsy monitoring and assistive technologies for people with disabilities. Zhu et al. (2024) proposed a hybrid SE-TCN-BiGRU network and reported high seizure-detection accuracy on the CHB-MIT and SH-SDU datasets. Garção et al. (2025) Developed a video-based approach for detecting seizures in real time using Lampsy, a non-intrusive monitoring solution powered by affordable edge devices. Research on assistive robotics highlights the potential of robots to support rehabilitation and interaction, while Milne-Ives et al. (2025) emphasised the underrepresentation of People with intellectual impairments participating in artificial intelligence research on epilepsy. Based on these findings, this study proposes a smart robotic assistant designed to support daily living through voice interaction, scheduled alerts, and seizure-event tracking. and caregiver notifications. The proposed system aims to provide personalised assistance through accessible interaction, privacy-conscious monitoring and human supervision. However, existing studies evaluate individual technologies rather than the complete proposed robot. Therefore, its effectiveness, usability and reliability cannot yet be assumed. Further development, user-centred testing and appropriate clinical evaluation are necessary to assess its practical benefits and safety. This study explores potential advancements and existing limitations in integrating intelligent seizure monitoring with socially assistive robotics to support people with intellectual disabilities and epilepsy.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Predictive Maintenance (PdM) is the model that brings together sensor data as well as systematic data analysis. Industry 4.0 is broadly using PdMs that are improving the applications of digitized information. The monitoring of the conditions of machine parts and various processes is the main goal of PdM because it predicts the occurrence of any possible failures and results in interventions to optimized maintenance. Nevertheless, rotational components employed in robotics are very important in terms of proactive maintenance. The applications of machine learning models to obtain real-time data and predict when a failure may occur long before the breakdown were the subject of our study. The predictive models are highly accurate on possible component malfunctions with a very reasonable accuracy. Random Forest offers a good accuracy of 92% whereas Neural Network model offers a better accuracy of 94%. These models are efficient as evidenced by their performance measures including precision, recall and the F1-score. These indicators focus on the capability of the model to identify timely component failures.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from the periphery of experimental computing to the centre of managerial practice, reshaping how organisations make decisions, allocate resources, engage customers and manage people. Despite the rapid growth of scholarship on the subject, the literature remains fragmented across functional silos, and the opportunities and risks of AI are frequently examined in isolation from one another. This conceptual study synthesises existing literature to examine the role of AI in modern business management and to articulate an integrated understanding of its opportunities and challenges. Drawing on the technology–organisation–environment framework, the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities theory and the automation–augmentation perspective, the paper develops a conceptual model comprising five interrelated components: AI adoption enablers, AI applications across management functions, the dual effects of AI (opportunities and challenges), organisational outcomes, and moderating governance mechanisms. The model proposes that AI generates sustainable value only when technological capability is matched by organisational readiness, responsible governance, effective human–AI collaboration and continuous workforce development. The discussion elaborates the implications of the model for strategic decision-making, operations, marketing, human resource management and finance, and considers the ethical, social and implementation challenges that accompany adoption. The paper contributes a theoretically grounded and integrative framework that can guide future empirical research and support managers who seek to adopt AI responsibly and effectively.

documents.abstract: The green and digital transitions do not automatically produce inclusive growth. They interact through distinct labour-market processes: green structural change reallocates employment across sectors and places, whereas artificial intelligence (AI) reorganises tasks and authority within workplaces. This article develops a process-based conceptual framework for examining when their interaction can support AI-enabled green growth. An integrative review brings together peer-reviewed research and recent comparative reports. The framework follows a directional sequence in which green restructuring and AI deployment generate sectoral reallocation and task/workplace reorganisation. Labour-market adjustment arrangements and structural context then shape how these mechanisms lead to environmental, productivity, employment, job-quality, and distributive outcomes. These elements are not specified as independent, dependent, mediator, or moderator variables because the article does not estimate a statistical model. The framework distinguishes an enabling pathway based on labour augmentation and shared productivity gains from an adverse pathway involving displacement, surveillance, unequal value capture, and ecological externalisation. Six propositions identify relationships for subsequent empirical examination. A renewable-electricity value-chain application illustrates why AI exposure and labour effects differ across manufacturing, construction, and operations. The contribution is a power-sensitive account that treats environmental improvement and decent work as joint and institutionally contingent outcomes.Keywords: twin transition, artificial intelligence, labour-market adaptation, just transition, green growth.

documents.abstract: Communication can feel intelligible, support competent action, or secure agreement while remaining poorly explained or unwarranted. This article introduces the Ubiquitous Sphoṭa–Pratibhā model to examine these divergences within situated meaning episodes. Comparative conceptual reconstruction brings Bhartṛhari’s linguistic wholeness and pratibhā into dialogue with communication theory, while distinguishing intrinsic reflexivity from reflective review. Sphoṭa and pratibhā identify structural and apprehensive perspectives on one episode of understanding, rather than successive processing stages. The model follows how apprehended import changes through formulation, public uptake and appraisal. It distinguishes experienced intelligibility, demonstrated grasp, articulation, coordination, warrant and fidelity to documented intention. A worked educational encounter shows how these achievements separate in human–AI communication. Four prospective propositions specify testable extensions and their possible failures. The contribution is an integrative architecture connecting lived understanding to public accountability; claims of additional predictive value remain open to comparison with cognitive and pragmatic alternatives.Keywords: communication theory; sphoṭa; pratibhā; consciousness; meaning; epistemic appraisal; human–AI communication

Abstract The "Provisional specification.pdf" introduces a comprehensive security architecture for governing autonomous artificial intelligence agents across isolated runtimes, administrative domains, and hardware environments. As AI agents increasingly invoke external tools and modify persistent data, the system distinguishes between an agent's ability to compute and its authority to execute consequential external effects. The architecture intercepts proposed agent operations, holding them in a non-effective state while a protected enforcement domain evaluates operation-specific authorization conditions and commits validation evidence. A scoped, non-bearer finality capability is then verified at an effectuation sink before the operation can produce real-world consequences. The specification covers advanced technical mechanisms including micro-virtual-machine isolation, task-preserving context minimization, distributed revocation, and hardware-level command accounting. Why You Should Download This Document You should download this specification if you are building, securing, or deploying autonomous AI agents that interact with enterprise resources, financial systems, or cloud infrastructure. It provides a detailed blueprint for preventing unauthorized external actions caused by prompt injection, compromised models, or hallucinated tool invocations. The document offers actionable implementations for deploying agents within virtual machines, micro-virtual machines, and OS-level containers while maintaining strict cryptographic and hardware-assisted oversight over API requests, network egress, and persistent memory mutations. Meta's newly launched Muse agent runs in isolated, secure virtual machines on the cloud to execute multi-step tasks across connected applications while attempting to limit unintended access to user credentials and ad systems. The specification provides a formalized, enterprise-grade extension of this concept, detailing how to implement micro-virtual-machine isolation and lifecycle-bound authority so that an agent's access to a tool connector does not automatically grant unrestricted execution rights. Similarly, as NVIDIA scales its AI hardware and NIM microservices for agentic workflows, the specification’s coverage of hardware-resident effect-budget accounting, accelerator-memory sanitization, and hardware queue containment offers a precise technical framework for securing agent workloads at the GPU and DPU layer

Working paper / critical narrative synthesis. Not peer reviewed. Volcanism should be understood as planetary infrastructure: a means by which internal activity supplies and renews surface environments, as well as a source of acute hazard. This paper argues that explaining Earth's long-term habitability requires placing volcanic processes within a coupled interior–surface system. Geological carbon cycling supplies the strongest mechanism, while stagnant-lid models, Venus, and the Lost City ecosystem distinguish supported mechanisms from universal necessity claims. The framework organizes the argument around supply, transformation, removal, and response time. This is a selective synthesis of published literature; it reports no new measurements, simulations, or independent model replications. Version 1.0 corrects and substantially revises the earlier web essay, including its claims about subduction, volatile delivery, extinction causation, and direct access to magma. Conjecture 7 for all n is not proved in this manuscript. For the Yellowstone permutation a (OEIS A098550), Conjecture 7 asserts a(n) <= (pi/2) n ln n for n >= 2; the earlier manuscripts of the series prove it for n >= n_0 with an ineffective n_0. This manuscript collects, as one account with proof sketches and references to the program's notes, the results on the conjecture for all n. (1) A certified computation (RC) of a(1), ..., a(N0), N0 = 8.3*10^10, by two programs whose hashes agree at 830 checkpoints on one machine; (RC) is a run certificate, not a proof, and gives Conjecture 7 for n <= N0. (2) A reduction: Conjecture 7 for all n follows from (RC), a hypothesis (NL) on primes (every prime r > 40,631,100,479 is normal, i.e. enters as 2r followed two steps later by r, and has entry index n_r >= 1.01 r), the riser law (S_LR) for t in the finite range [N0, e^143) only (e^143 is about 10^62), and computed tables (DATA; certified except one floating-point table; one interval re-certification assumes the platform libm within 4 ulp). (NL) quantifies over all large primes, so this is not a finite-range reduction; only the height input has been confined to a finite range. (3) A height theorem: under the hypotheses of the program's Lemma LIN-ROUGH, a(n) <= (pi/2) n ln n at every composite-anchored step with ln n >= 143 (certified cells up to ln n = 10^7 and an analytic tail beyond), proved by forcing too many risers. (4) From (RC) and refereed lemmas alone, every prime in (40,631,100,479, 4.105*10^10] is normal, and no prime in (40,631,100,479, 4.2583*10^10] enters as 3r. (5) For primes p > 40,631,100,479 with q_p = 2, under normality of the primes below p, the run data and the floating-point table of GIILE, the entry bound (LE*) holds at every such p <= 1.6503*10^11 for every entry mask, and below 10^300 a failure needs a "core lock" of consecutive entry masks. (6) With no normality, run or stock input, n_P >= 0.7444 P for every prime P > exp(2*10^452); this proof has no numerics referee, uses floating-point data, two of its inputs were refereed only once, and the threshold rests on a stated modification of the proofs (the exact band parameter H). The manuscript also records where the height method stops: its yield cap is at most 0.863 at N0 and exceeds 1 stably only from ln n about 29.4 (uncertified double-precision values), so this family of bounds cannot reach N0.
